title: [BUG] Scorer versioning docs describe OSS behavior, register() raises ValueError on Databricks tracking URI
body:
<!-- issue-warning -->
> [!WARNING]
> Before submitting a PR, please make sure that:
> - A maintainer has triaged this issue and applied the `ready` label
> - This issue has no assignee
> - No duplicate PR exists
>
> PRs not meeting these requirements may be automatically closed.

### Issues Policy acknowledgement

- [x] I have read and agree to submit bug reports in accordance with the [issues policy](https://www.github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/master/ISSUE_POLICY.md)

### Where did you encounter this bug?

Databricks

### MLflow version

Verified against `main` branch on 2026-06-25. The behavior is present in current released versions on Databricks tracking URIs.

### Describe the problem

The docs page at [`docs/docs/genai/eval-monitor/scorers/versioning.mdx`](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/main/docs/docs/genai/eval-monitor/scorers/versioning.mdx) says:

> Registering a new scorer with the same name will create a new version.

This is true on the OSS MLflow tracking backend (`MlflowTrackingStore`). The test at `tests/genai/scorers/test_scorer_CRUD.py::test_mlflow_backend_scorer_operations` confirms it (`assert len(scorer_versions) == 2` after two `register()` calls with the same name).

On a Databricks tracking URI, the same flow raises a `ValueError`. The Databricks scorer backend does not support versioning.

From [`mlflow/genai/scorers/registry.py`](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/main/mlflow/genai/scorers/registry.py) on `main`:

- `DatabricksStore.register_scorer()` calls `databricks.agents.scorers.add_scheduled_scorer`. That transitively calls `databricks-rag-eval`, which raises:
  ```
  ValueError: A scorer with name '<name>' has already been registered.
  Update the scorer using '.update()' or choose a different name.
  ```
  Source: `databricks/rag_eval/monitoring/scheduled_scorers.py:122-128`. The inline comment in the same block reads `# Error message reflects how MLflow uses this function`, which suggests the package authors knew MLflow users would hit this.
- `DatabricksStore.list_scorer_versions()` raises `MlflowException("Scorer DatabricksStore does not support versioning.")`.
- `DatabricksStore.get_scorer(version=...)` and `DatabricksStore.delete_scorer(version=...)` both reject the version parameter.

The versioning docs page doesn't surface this. Users on Databricks following the page hit the ValueError on the second `register()` call.

Separately, the docs example on the same page uses `model="anthropic:/claude-opus-4-1-20250805"`, which `Scorer.register()` also rejects on Databricks via `_check_can_be_registered` in `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py:1130`:

> `MlflowException: The scorer's judge model must use Databricks as a model provider in order to be registered or updated. Please use the default judge model or specify a model value starting with 'databricks:/'. Got anthropic:/claude-opus-4-1-20250805.`

So the docs example itself does not execute as written on a Databricks tracking URI.

Surfaced by a teammate hitting it on a Databricks workspace while following the docs verbatim.

### Code to reproduce issue

```python
import mlflow
from mlflow.genai.judges import make_judge

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("databricks")
mlflow.set_experiment("my-experiment")
exp_id = mlflow.get_experiment_by_name("my-experiment").experiment_id

j = make_judge(
    name="response_quality",
    instructions="Evaluate if {{ outputs }} is high quality for {{ inputs }}.",
    feedback_value_type=str,
)
j.register(experiment_id=exp_id)

j2 = make_judge(
    name="response_quality",
    instructions="Updated instructions. Evaluate {{ outputs }} for {{ inputs }}.",
    feedback_value_type=str,
)
j2.register(experiment_id=exp_id)
# raises ValueError on Databricks
# creates a second version on OSS tracking server
```

### Stack trace

```
ValueError: A scorer with name 'response_quality' has already been registered.
Update the scorer using '.update()' or choose a different name.

  File "mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py", line 835, in register
    store.register_scorer(experiment_id, new_scorer)
  File "mlflow/genai/scorers/registry.py", line 435, in register_scorer
    DatabricksStore.add_registered_scorer(...)
  File "databricks/rag_eval/monitoring/scheduled_scorers.py", line 126, in add_scheduled_scorer
    raise ValueError(...)
```

Reproduced end-to-end on Databricks workspace.

### Suggested fix

Two layered:

1. **Docs accuracy.** Update `versioning.mdx` to state that SDK-based versioning is supported on the OSS tracking backend but not on Databricks tracking URIs. List the workarounds the Databricks error message already implies:
   - In-place update via `Scorer.update(...)` (the path the error message points to)
   - Delete and re-register (no history)
   - Version the instruction template via Prompt Registry and load it from a single judge (preserves instruction history)
2. **Docs example correctness.** Replace the `model="anthropic:/claude-opus-4-1-20250805"` line in the SDK example with either no `model` argument (default judge model) or a `databricks:/` model URI, so the example executes on Databricks tracking URIs.
3. **UX improvement.** In `DatabricksStore.register_scorer()`, wrap the transitive `ValueError` from `databricks-rag-eval` into an `MlflowException` with the same guidance. Gives users a consistent MlflowException at the MLflow API boundary instead of a downstream package error. Small and additive.

### What component(s) does this bug affect?

- [x] `area/docs`: MLflow documentation pages
- [x] `area/evaluation`: MLflow model evaluation features, evaluation metrics, and evaluation workflows

title: [DOC-FIX] Wrong EvaluationDataset type referenced in LLMs & Agents Docs
body: > [!WARNING] > Before submitting a PR, please make sure that: > - A maintainer has triaged this issue and applied the `ready` label > - This issue has no assignee > - No duplicate PR exists > > PRs not meeting these requirements may be automatically closed. ### Willingness to contribute Yes. I can contribute a documentation fix independently. ### URL(s) with the issue https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/concepts/evaluation-datasets/ ### Description of proposal (what needs changing) The `EvaluationDataset` Dataset Structure page type referenced and documented in the [Evaluation Dataset Concepts](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/concepts/evaluation-datasets/) docs under LLMs & Agents is referring to the `EvaluationDataset` type defined in ```python mlflow.entities.evaluation_dataset.py ``` However, the documentation on the previous page, [Building MLflow evaluation datasets](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/datasets/) shows the evaluation dataset created with `create_dataset` under the genai sub-module. ```python from mlflow.genai.datasets import create_dataset ``` This function creates an object of type ```python mlflow.genai.datasets.evaluation_dataset.EvaluationDataset ``` which has a very different implementation than the one under `mlflow.entities`. For example, the `records` property is not present. This could be a simple documentation update where the schema breakdown needs to reference this other type. However, this could also indicate the intention to migrate the GenAI `EvaluationDataset` and the one under entities to match. The doc string under the mlflow.entities: ```python class EvaluationDataset(_MlflowObject, Dataset, PyFuncConvertibleDatasetMixin): """ Evaluation dataset for storing inputs and expectations for GenAI evaluation. This class supports lazy loading of records - when retrieved via get_evaluation_dataset(), only metadata is loaded. Records are fetched when to_df() or merge_records() is called. """ ``` But the current genai `EvaluationDataset` better resembles the one under `mlflow.data.evaluation_dataset` ```python class EvaluationDataset: """ An input dataset for model evaluation. This is intended for use with the :py:func:`mlflow.models.evaluate()` API. """ ``` Ultimately, when creating genai evaluation datasets and exploring properties this is very confusing. The intended `create_dataset` function creates a different object than what is documented.

title: Docs: Add IAM permissions and AWS region setup for Amazon Bedrock (Nova models)
body:
### Willingness to contribute

Yes. I can contribute a documentation fix independently.

### URL(s) with the issue

https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/eval-monitor/scorers/llm-judge/


### Description of proposal (what needs changing)

The current GenAI / Bedrock documentation shows how to use Amazon Bedrock models
(e.g., Amazon Nova) with MLflow, but it does not clearly document:

- Required AWS IAM permissions for Bedrock model invocation
- How to configure the AWS region for Bedrock usage
- Common errors users encounter when permissions or regions are misconfigured

This often leads to errors like `AccessDeniedException` or region mismatch issues
for first-time users.

Proposed improvement:

Add a short section that includes:
- Minimal IAM policy required for Amazon Bedrock access
- Example of setting the AWS region (environment variable or config)
- A small “Common Errors” section explaining typical permission/region failures

I’m happy to submit a PR with these documentation updates.

title: [DOC-FIX] Update MLflow Tracking Quickstart: local server must use database-backed backend to register models
body:
### Willingness to contribute

Yes. I can contribute a documentation fix independently.

### URL(s) with the issue

https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/ml/tracking/quickstart/

### Description of proposal (what needs changing)

The MLflow Tracking Quickstart instructs users to start a local tracking server with:

```
mlflow server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

and then set the tracking URI to that server and register a model using `mlflow.sklearn.log_model(..., registered_model_name="tracking-quickstart", ...)`. When following these instructions on a local machine with MLflow 3.1, the `log_model` call fails with a 404 error (`API request to endpoint /api/2.0/mlflow/logged-models failed with error code 404`). This happens because the local tracking server is configured with the default file-based backend store, which does not support Model Registry or logged model APIs. According to the MLflow Tracking documentation, "To use the Model Registry functionality with MLflow tracking, you must use database backed store such as PostgresQL".

The Quickstart should either instruct users to run the tracking server with a database-backed backend (e.g. `--backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db`) or omit the `registered_model_name` and `set_logged_model_tags` calls when using the default file-based store. Without this clarification, newcomers following the quickstart encounter a confusing error.

I propose updating the Quickstart documentation as follows:

* In **Step 2 – Start a Tracking Server**, add a note that registering a model requires a database-backed backend store. Provide an example command such as:

```
mlflow server --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

and mention that for a simple file-backed server, users should remove the `registered_model_name` parameter and skip setting logged model tags.

* Alternatively, separate the Quickstart into two variants: one for logging a model without registration (works with the default file store) and another for registering a model that uses a database-backed tracking server.

This update will prevent the `logged-models` 404 error and align the quickstart with the Model Registry requirements in the MLflow documentation.

title: [FR] Add "ranker" model_type support to mlflow.evaluate()
body:
### Willingness to contribute

Yes. I would be willing to contribute this feature with guidance from the MLflow community.

### Proposal Summary

I'd like to propose adding support for a new `model_type` called "ranker" to mlflow.evaluate() for ML problems where the evaluation set is broken up into groups of "queries" with scored "items" that need to be ranked _within each group_. This feature would allow MLflow to natively support the evaluation of ranking and recommendation models by providing essential metrics like NDCG, MAP@K, and MRR. Currently, users need external tools for these evaluations, but integrating "ranker" would streamline workflows and make MLflow a more comprehensive platform for the entire machine learning lifecycle specifically for ranking problems.

### Motivation

> #### What is the use case for this feature?

This feature primarily addresses the need for comprehensive and standardized evaluation of ranking models within consumer-facing applications. For products like e-commerce search, personalized content feeds, or streaming service recommendations, the quality of a ranked list directly impacts user engagement and satisfaction. Data scientists and ML engineers currently lack a native, integrated method within MLflow to evaluate these models using critical ranking-specific metrics (e.g., NDCG, MAP@K, MRR), leading to fragmented workflows and hindering rapid iteration on critical user-facing features.

> #### Why is this use case valuable to support for MLflow users in general?

Supporting this use case is valuable for MLflow users in general because it significantly expands MLflow's utility to a major segment of the ML ecosystem and promotes best practices for MLOps.

1. Broadens MLflow's Scope: Ranking and recommendation systems are ubiquitous in modern applications. By supporting a "ranker" model_type, MLflow becomes a more complete and versatile platform, enabling a much wider array of ML practitioners to manage their entire ML lifecycle within a single tool. This attracts new users who previously found MLflow lacking in this area.
2. Standardizes MLOps for Ranking: Currently, evaluating ranking models often involves disparate tools. This leads to inconsistent evaluation methodologies, difficulty in comparing experiments, and increased operational overhead. Integrating ranking evaluation into mlflow.evaluate() would provide a standardized, opinionated approach, promoting reproducibility and reducing cognitive load for users.
4. Accelerates Experimentation and Deployment: When evaluation is integrated, users can more quickly iterate on model improvements, compare different algorithms (e.g., neural ranking models vs. tree-based models), and confidently select the best-performing model for deployment. This directly translates to faster innovation cycles and quicker delivery of improved user experiences.
6. Enhances Model Observability and Auditability: By logging ranking metrics directly within MLflow Tracking using mlflow.evaluate() natively, users gain a centralized view of their model's performance over time and across different runs. This improves observability, makes it easier to audit model behavior, and aids in debugging and performance regression analysis.
7. Reduces Tool Sprawl: MLflow's value proposition is to provide a comprehensive platform. By absorbing a common evaluation need currently met by external tools, it helps users consolidate their MLOps stack, reducing complexity and maintenance burden.

> #### Why is this use case valuable to support for your project(s) or organization?

For our organization, which has many ML ranking applications powering our personalization systems, the inability to use mlflow.evaluate() for these specific problems creates a critical gap in our otherwise standardized ML lifecycle.

Here's why supporting this use case is critically valuable for us:

1. Bridging the mlflow.evaluate() Gap for Ranking: We extensively use MLflow for all other aspects of our model lifecycle – from experiment tracking and parameter logging to model registry and deployment. However, when it comes to evaluating our ranking models, we hit a wall. mlflow.evaluate() currently does not support the necessary ranking metrics or data structures, forcing us out of the MLflow ecosystem precisely at the evaluation stage. This feature would close this critical gap, allowing us to leverage the convenience and automation of mlflow.evaluate() for all our ML problems, including ranking.
3. Driving True End-to-End MLflow Standardization: The lack of native ranking evaluation means our ML project pipelines are not fully standardized across the organization. For ranking problems, we are presently forced to leverage external tools like Evidently to compute metrics and create custom visualizations. This creates a dual workflow: one streamlined within MLflow for classification/regression, and another fragmented one for ranking. Implementing "ranker" model_type in mlflow.evaluate() would drive genuine end-to-end standardization of our ML project pipelines across our entire organization.
5. Significant Reduction in ML Practitioner Cognitive Load and Overhead: Our data scientists and ML engineers experience considerable friction due to this missing capability. They must:
- Learn and maintain separate, non-MLflow specific evaluation code for ranking.
- Perform manual data transformations to fit external tool requirements.
- Explicitly write code to re-log metrics and artifacts from these external tools back into MLflow, if they want them tracked. This "context switching" and manual work increase cognitive load and development overhead. By enabling mlflow.evaluate() for ranking, we can drastically reduce this burden, allowing our practitioners to focus on model development rather than evaluation pipeline plumbing.
10. Enhanced Comparability and Reproducibility for Critical Ranking Models: With a standardized mlflow.evaluate() process for ranking, we would gain immediate benefits in comparing different ranking model iterations side-by-side in the MLflow UI, ensuring consistent evaluation criteria. This is paramount for our ranking applications where small improvements in ranking quality can lead to significant business impact.

> #### Why is it currently difficult to achieve this use case?

It is currently difficult to achieve this use case primarily because MLflow's existing mlflow.evaluate() capabilities are designed for classification and regression problems among others, and inherently lack the specialized understanding of group-based ranking as far as I can tell.

Here's why related MLflow features are insufficient:

1. mlflow.evaluate()'s model_type limitations:

### Proposal Summary

Newer versions of langchain allow you to specify `response_format: Literal["content", "content_and_artifact"]` when creating tools. These produce tool messages with an additional `artifact` field: https://python.langchain.com/docs/concepts/messages/#toolmessage. The artifact field is helpful for ensuring any metadata from the tool is returned without being passed to the LLM in the agent

When we use ChatAgentToolNode it will parse a dictionary with keys: "content", "attachments" and "custom_outputs" but it would improve the dx if it could parse the `artifact` attribute of the ToolMessage and allow us to store a serialized version in the attachments or similar


The current solution I have is to create a CustomChatAgentToolNode, similar to ChatAgentToolNode with the following change:

Original `invoke` method:
 ```python
    def invoke(self, input: Input, config: Optional[RunnableConfig] = None, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        """
        Wraps the standard ToolNode invoke method to:
        - Parse ChatAgentState into LangChain messages
        - Parse dictionary string outputs from both UC function and standard LangChain python tools
          that include keys ``content``, ``attachments``, and ``custom_outputs``.
        """
        messages = input["messages"]
        for msg in messages:
            for tool_call in msg.get("tool_calls", []):
                tool_call["name"] = tool_call["function"]["name"]
                tool_call["args"] = json.loads(tool_call["function"]["arguments"])
        input["messages"] = convert_to_messages(messages)

        result = super().invoke(input, config, **kwargs)

        messages = []
        custom_outputs = None
        for m in result["messages"]:
            try:
                return_obj = json.loads(m.content)
                if all(key in return_obj for key in ("format", "value", "truncated")):
                    # Dictionary output with custom_outputs and attachments from a UC function
                    try:
                        return_obj = json.loads(return_obj["value"])
                    except Exception:
                        pass
                if "custom_outputs" in return_obj:
                    custom_outputs = return_obj["custom_outputs"]
                if m.id is None:
                    m.id = str(uuid4())
                messages.append(parse_message(m, attachments=return_obj.get("attachments")))
            except Exception:
                messages.append(parse_message(m))
        return {"messages": messages, "custom_outputs": custom_outputs}
```

### Proposal Summary

Add a Skill Registry to MLflow: a governed, metadata-first registry for
AI agent skills. The registry stores metadata and typed source pointers
(to Git repos, OCI registries, ZIP archives, etc.) rather than skill
artifacts directly. This provides enterprise governance (lifecycle
management, security scan tracking, usage analytics) on top of existing
skill distribution mechanisms, without replacing them.

The registry also introduces skill groups, allowing related skills to be
organized into coherent toolboxes or workflows and discovered as a unit.

### Motivation

#### What is the use case for this feature?

Organizations adopting agentic AI need to govern skills across teams.
GitHub is sufficient for skill development and versioning, but
enterprises need a governance layer on top: publish-state lifecycle
(draft/published/deprecated/retired), security scan tracking, federated
discovery across multiple distribution mechanisms, and skill grouping
for related capabilities.

#### Why is this use case valuable to support for MLflow users in general?

MLflow is already the natural place to manage versioned AI assets. The MCP Server Registry proposal ([#22625](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/issues/22625)) establishes the pattern for governed, metadata-first AI asset registries in MLflow. A skill registry is the next concrete instance of this pattern. As agentic AI workflows grow, skills become as important to govern as models and MCP servers.

#### Why is this use case valuable to support for your project(s) or organization?

Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) customers in regulated environments need
governed skill management with multi-tenancy isolation, security scan
tracking, and support for multiple distribution mechanisms including OCI.
The metadata-first approach lets the registry work regardless of where
skill content is stored.

#### Why is it currently difficult to achieve this use case?

There is no standard way to record a skill's publish state, security
scan results, or group membership alongside its version history. MLflow
traces can capture some skill metadata, but there is no governed
registry to link that trace data back to.

body:
### Willingness to contribute

Yes. I can contribute this feature independently.

### Proposal Summary

Add S3 object tagging support for MLflow artifact uploads to enable cost tracking and resource management.
## 1. Problem Statement
Organizations using MLflow with S3 artifact storage need to track and allocate costs for artifact uploads across 
different teams, projects. Currently, MLflow uploads artifacts to S3 without any tagging mechanism, making it difficult to:

• **Cost Attribution**: Track S3 storage and transfer costs by team, project.
• **Resource Management**: Identify which artifacts belong to specific cost centers or billing accounts
• **Compliance Requirements**: Meet organizational tagging policies for cloud resources
• **Budget Monitoring**: Set up cost alerts and budgets based on artifact usage patterns

## 2. Proposed Solution
Add optional S3 object tagging support to MLflow artifact uploads:

• **Custom tagging only**: Allow users to specify S3 tags via environment variables
• **Automatic tag injection**: Apply tags to all artifact uploads across all upload methods
• **Transparent to users**: Tags automatically applied when calling log_artifact() and log_artifacts()
• **Backward compatibility**: Feature is optional and disabled by default

### Motivation

> #### What is the use case for this feature?
Enterprise organizations need to track and allocate S3 costs for MLflow artifacts across different teams, 
projects, and cost centers. Without tagging, all artifact storage appears as undifferentiated S3 costs, making it 
impossible to:
• Charge back storage costs to appropriate teams
• Set up cost alerts for specific projects
• Comply with organizational cloud resource tagging policies
• Monitor artifact storage growth by experiment or user

> #### Why is this use case valuable to support for MLflow users in general?
Cost visibility and resource management are critical for enterprise MLflow adoption. Many organizations have 
strict requirements for cloud resource tagging to enable proper cost allocation and governance.

> #### Why is this use case valuable to support for your project(s) or organization?
Our customers frequently request this capability for budget tracking and compliance. They need to allocate MLflow 
artifact storage costs to specific teams and projects for accurate cost accounting.

> #### Why is it currently difficult to achieve this use case?
MLflow doesn't provide any mechanism to add S3 object tags during artifact uploads. Users would need to implement 
custom post-processing scripts to tag artifacts after upload, which is inefficient and doesn't capture all upload 
scenarios.



### Details

### 4. Design

#### 4.1 Configuration Management
Environment Variables:
• MLFLOW_S3_ARTIFACT_TAGGING_ENABLED: Enable/disable tagging (default: false)
• MLFLOW_S3_ARTIFACT_TAGS: JSON string of custom tags {"cost_center": "ml-team", "project": "recommendation"}

#### 4.2 Implementation Components

File: mlflow/store/artifact/s3_artifact_repo.py
• Add centralized _get_upload_tags() method to read environment variables and generate tags
• Modify _upload_file() to include Tagging parameter for direct uploads
• Update create_multipart_upload() to include tags in multipart initiation
• Update create_presigned_upload_url() to include tagging in presigned URL generation
• Apply tags consistently across all S3 upload methods

File: mlflow/server/handlers.py
• Modify upload_artifact_handler() to apply tags in --serve-artifacts mode

File: mlflow/environment_variables.py
• Add new environment variables for tagging configuration
• Include validation for tag format and AWS tag limits (max 10 tags, key/value length limits)

#### 4.3 Tag Application by Upload Method
• **Direct uploads**: s3_client.upload_file() with ExtraArgs={'Tagging': tag_string}
• **Multipart uploads**: create_multipart_upload() with Tagging parameter
• **Presigned URLs**: Include Tagging parameter and x-amz-tagging header
• **Serve-artifacts mode**: Apply tags in server-side upload logic

#### 4.4 User Experience
Transparent integration: Users continue using log_artifact() and log_artifacts() APIs without code changes. Tags 
are automatically applied when environment variables are configured.

export MLFLOW_S3_ARTIFACT_TAGGING_ENABLED=true

title: [Feature Request]: (Truely) Multimodal Embeddings
body:
### Feature Description

In the past, multimodal embeddings meant having a separate vector space for each modality. From [this discussion](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/10486#issuecomment-2770873498), I understand that this has been discussed and is not yet supported fully as it would require significant change to llama-index-code.

However, recently we are seeing more and more embedding models that support embedding a sequence of interleaved modalities jointly. Just like LlamaIndex now supports this for the ChatMessage class. The format that I saw for Cohere and Voyage embedding models was:
```python
image = requests.get("https://cohere.com/favicon-32x32.png")
url = f"data:{image.headers['Content-Type']};base64,{base64.b64encode(image.content).decode('utf-8')}"
image_inputs = [
    {
        "content": [
            {"type": "text", "text": "Look at this:"},
            {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": url}},
        ]
    }
]
```

I think support for this would be pretty valuable and is probably achieveable without having to change ALL embedding model implementations at once.
It should be possible to introduce a new `MixedNode` or something alongside the `Node`, `TextNode`  and `ImageNode`, etc. that stores content in a comparable format. In the `BaseEmbedding` class, adjustments to `__call__`, `acall` and the corresponding new methods for mixed modality embeddings would be required. And then lastly, a check by the node type could be used to route the content accordingly.
For the sake of consistency with your decisions regarding the merge of `MultiModalLLM` into the `LLM` implementation, this would also enable slowly moving away from `MultiModalEmbedding`.

I'd be happy to draft a PR for this, if you confirm that the approach I lined out sounds valid and that I did not overlook any major showstoppers!

Kind regards
Enrico

title: bug: dataset_run_items.create race condition causes unique constraint violation on datasetRuns(dataset_id, project_id, name)
body:
## Describe the bug

When calling `dataset.run_experiment()` with `max_concurrency > 1` on a fresh `run_name`, multiple concurrent items each try to create the same dataset run via `api.dataset_run_items.create()`. The backend Prisma layer appears to call `datasetRuns.create()` directly (not upsert), so all items except one fail with:

```
prisma:error
Invalid `prisma.datasetRuns.create()` invocation:
Unique constraint failed on the fields: (`dataset_id`,`project_id`,`name`)
```

In the Python SDK these surface as repeated log lines:

```
ERROR [langfuse] Failed to create dataset run item: Unique constraint failed on the fields: (`dataset_id`,`project_id`,`name`)
```

Net effect: the dataset run gets created by the first winner, but the remaining N-1 items lose their link to the run (no `dataset_run_item` row), so the run appears incomplete in the UI even though all traces are emitted correctly.

## To reproduce

```python
from langfuse import Langfuse, Evaluation

client = Langfuse(host="...", public_key="...", secret_key="...")
dataset = client.get_dataset("orchestrator-smoke")  # 28 items

def task(*, item, **kwargs):
    return {"echo": (item.input or {}).get("q", "")[:40]}

def scorer(*, input, output, expected_output, metadata, **kwargs):
    return [Evaluation(name="dummy", value=1.0)]

# Fails with multiple unique-constraint errors:
dataset.run_experiment(
    name="repro",
    run_name="repro-run-1",   # fresh run_name
    task=task,
    evaluators=[scorer],
    max_concurrency=5,         # >1 triggers the race
)
```

Setting `max_concurrency=1` makes the issue disappear because only one item attempts to create the run.

## Expected behavior

`api.dataset_run_items.create` should upsert the parent `dataset_run` when `run_name` is new, so N parallel callers all converge to the same `dataset_run_id` instead of racing on `create`.

Alternatively, the SDK could pre-create the run once before fanning out items.

## Environment

- Self-hosted `langfuse/langfuse:3.175.0` (latest v3 as of 2026-05-21)
- Worker `langfuse/langfuse-worker:3`
- ClickHouse + Postgres + Redis + MinIO (standard v3 stack)
- Python SDK: `langfuse==4.6.1`
- Python: 3.11

## Workaround

`max_concurrency=1` serializes all `dataset_run_items.create` calls so the first creates the run and the rest reuse it. Cost: experiments run serially instead of in parallel.

title: bug(worker): ClickhouseWriter drops rows after max flush attempts with no DLQ
body:
### Describe the bug

`ClickhouseWriter` buffers inserts in an in-memory queue and flushes either on a timer or when the batch reaches `LANGFUSE_INGESTION_CLICKHOUSE_WRITE_BATCH_SIZE`. If a flush fails, records are pushed back onto the queue with their `attempts` counter incremented. Once `attempts` is no longer **strictly less than** `LANGFUSE_INGESTION_CLICKHOUSE_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (default: **3**), those rows are permanently removed from memory and discarded. At that point, only logs and the `langfuse.queue.clickhouse_writer.error` metric remain. There is currently no durable dead-letter queue (DLQ) or automatic replay mechanism implemented for this path (the code itself contains a TODO referencing Redis-backed dead-lettering).

Several ingestion and processing flows call `addToQueue()` asynchronously and do not wait for a successful ClickHouse write before considering the operation complete. As a result, a **successful BullMQ job does not guarantee that data was durably written to ClickHouse**.

Under repeated insert failures — for example:

- ClickHouse downtime
- network interruptions
- persistent schema or validation issues
- malformed payloads
- partial cluster failures

— batches can silently age out of retry attempts and be dropped entirely. This can lead to **permanent loss of traces, observations, scores, and other ClickHouse-backed entities**, even though upstream ingestion or processing jobs appear successful from the application's perspective.

**Expected:** Failed ClickHouse writes should either:
- retry with bounded backpressure and durable persistence, or
- be moved to a durable DLQ (or equivalent replayable store) for later recovery.

Additionally, user-visible “ingestion succeeded” semantics should align with the point at which data is actually durable in ClickHouse.

**Actual:** After the configured retry limit is reached, failed batches are dropped from in-memory state with no built-in replay or recovery path.

---

### Steps to reproduce

1. **Unit test reproduction (minimal, no real ClickHouse required)**  
   - Open `worker/src/services/ClickhouseWriter/ClickhouseWriter.unit.test.ts`
   - Run the test:
     - `should drop records after max attempts`
   - The test mocks `insert()` to always reject, repeatedly advances the flush timer until `maxAttempts` is exhausted, and verifies:
     - the queue becomes empty, and
     - logs contain:
       - `"Max attempts reached"`

2. **Runtime / integration-style reproduction**
   - Start the worker with ClickHouse unavailable or intentionally misconfigured
     - alternatively, mock the ClickHouse client so `insert()` always fails
   - Trigger any workflow that calls `ClickhouseWriter.addToQueue()`
     - e.g. ingestion paths using `IngestionService.mergeAndWrite`
   - Observe logs such as:
     - `ClickhouseWriter.flush`
     - `ClickhouseWriter: Max attempts reached`
   - Confirm:
     - ingestion/BullMQ jobs may still complete successfully
     - affected rows never appear in ClickHouse
     - no automatic replay occurs

---

### Langfuse Cloud or self-hosted?

Self-hosted

---

### If self-hosted, what version are you running?

`git describe: v3.172.1-14-g60fee25fd-dirty`  
`commit: 60fee25fd`

---

### SDK and integration versions

N/A for this report

---

### Additional information

#### Relevant implementation locations

- **Writer implementation:**  
  `worker/src/services/ClickhouseWriter/index.ts`
  - `flush()` catch block:
    - retries by re-queueing with incremented `attempts`
    - drops rows after retry exhaustion
  - `addToQueue()`:
    - only enqueues data
    - does not await durable ClickHouse persistence

- **Configuration defaults:**  
  `worker/src/env.ts`
  - `LANGFUSE_INGESTION_CLICKHOUSE_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (default: `3`)
  - `LANGFUSE_INGESTION_CLICKHOUSE_WRITE_INTERVAL_MS`
  - `LANGFUSE_INGESTION_CLICKHOUSE_WRITE_BATCH_SIZE`

---

#### Observability when drops occur

- **Metric**
  - `langfuse.queue.clickhouse_writer.error`

- **Logs**
  - `ClickhouseWriter.flush`
  - `ClickhouseWriter: Max attempts reached, dropped ...`
    - includes a partial list of `droppedIds`

---

#### Related gaps

- `worker/src/services/dlq/dlqRetryService.ts`
  - currently does not include ingestion or ClickHouse-writer retry handling
  - only other queue types are covered

- Existing TODO in `ClickhouseWriter`
  - references dead-lettering to Redis instead of dropping records

---

#### Ingestion note (mitigation, not a fix)

Standard ingestion paths store original payloads in S3 via:
- `worker/src/queues/ingestionQueue.ts`

This may allow manual replay if:
- S3 retention is enabled, and
- replay tooling/processes exist.

However:
- `ClickhouseWriter` itself has no automatic replay capability, and
- other `addToQueue()` call sites may not benefit from the same S3-backed recovery path.

---

### Suggested fix directions (for discussion)

- Introduce a durable DLQ for failed ClickHouse batches
  - store either full payloads or replay references/pointers
- Provide a supported replay workflow/tooling path
- Revisit ingestion success semantics so “success” reflects durable persistence guarantees
- Consider surfacing explicit partial-ingestion or ClickHouse-write failure states
- Reevaluate retry classification behavior
  - `isRetryableError()` currently appears narrow
  - transient transport/network failures may not behave predictably under current retry handling

---

### Where did you encounter this bug?

Other

### MLflow version

- Client: 3.10.1
- Tracking server: 3.10.1


### System information

- **OS Platform and Distribution (e.g., Linux Ubuntu 16.04)**: debian:12-slim
- **Python version**: 3.13.7
- mlflow server is running on azure web server using mlflow server

### Describe the problem

## Bug Report: Online Evaluator misses traces with duration > scheduler interval (Race Condition)

### System Information
* **MLflow Version:** 3.10.1
* **Task Queue:** Huey (as seen in server logs)
* **Environment:** Tracking Server with GenAI Automatic Evaluation enabled.

### Describe the Problem
The `mlflow.server.jobs.utils.online_scoring_scheduler` uses a strictly forward-moving time window based on a trace's **start time** (`trace.timestamp_ms`). Because my evaluator filters for `trace.status = 'OK'`, any trace whose execution time exceeds the scheduler's scan frequency (or falls across a window boundary while still `IN_PROGRESS`) is systematically ignored and never evaluated.

### Evidence & Log Analysis
1. **The Scheduler Scan:** At `15:22:07`, the scheduler scans the window `[1774020058433, 1774020127815]`.
   * Log: `Fetching traces with filter: trace.timestamp_ms >= ... AND trace.status = 'OK'`
   * **Result:** `Fetched 0 trace infos`.

2. **The Trace Execution:** Trace `tr-0199236e2d678bcf22641153809d27fb` has an execution time of **74.133s**. 
   * It started within the window above, but it did not finish until `15:22:55` (as evidenced by the `POST /api/3.0/mlflow/traces` log).
   * While the scheduler was scanning its "start window" at `15:22:07`, the trace status was still `IN_PROGRESS`.

3. **The Window Skip:** At `15:23:02`, the scheduler moves to the next window: `[1774020127815, 1774020182053]`.
   * Because the trace's start timestamp is `1774020058433`, it is now **outside the current window**.
   * Even though the trace is now `OK`, the scheduler will never look back at that timestamp range again.

4. **Confirmation:** A manual query using the exact same filters *after completion* successfully returns the trace, proving it was only missing during the scheduler's specific execution time due to the status filter.

```
trace = client.search_traces(locations=['30'], max_results=1, filter_string="trace.timestamp_ms >= 1774020058433 AND trace.timestamp_ms <= 1774020127815 AND metadata.mlflow.sourceRun IS NULL AND trace.status = 'OK'")
print(trace)
[Trace(trace_id=tr-0199236e2d678bcf22641153809d27fb)]
```

### Expected Behavior
The automatic evaluator should account for traces that started in a previous window but finished late. This could be solved by:
1.  **Lookback Buffer:** Allowing the scheduler to scan overlapping windows or a "grace period" (e.g., scan the last 5 minutes every 1 minute).
2.  **Status-Based Retries:** Re-scanning traces that were marked `IN_PROGRESS` in the previous cycle once they reach `OK` status.
3.  **Configurable Scan Delay:** Providing a documented and functional environment variable to offset the "window end" relative to current time.

### Actual Behavior
Traces that take longer than ~60 seconds to execute are permanently skipped by the automatic scoring logic, leaving evaluation metrics as `null` in the UI.

    trace_id = trace.info.request_id

title: Span processor ignores OpenInference's `llm.cost.total` attribute; recomputes from partial `llm.token_count.*` instead
body:
## Summary

When tracing the Anthropic Claude Agent SDK via the [OpenInference Claude Agent SDK instrumentation](https://github.com/Arize-ai/openinference/tree/main/js/packages/openinference-instrumentation-claude-agent-sdk) + `@langfuse/otel`, the **authoritative LLM cost is correctly captured as the OTel attribute `llm.cost.total` on the AGENT span**, but Langfuse ignores it and displays a derived cost from `llm.token_count.*` × the pricing table. That derived value is materially under-counted (~40% of actual) because the OpenInference instrumentation only emits the last-turn input tokens + total output tokens — it does not emit `llm.token_count.prompt_cache_read` or `llm.token_count.prompt_cache_creation`, which dominate input usage on multi-turn agent runs that use Anthropic prompt caching.

Expected: when an OTel span carries `llm.cost.total`, Langfuse should use that as the authoritative cost (or, at minimum, surface it alongside the computed value and let users prefer it). Today it's silently dropped.

## Reproduction

Setup per [docs/integrations/claude-agent-sdk-js](https://langfuse.com/integrations/frameworks/claude-agent-sdk-js):

```ts
import { NodeSDK } from "@opentelemetry/sdk-node";
import { LangfuseSpanProcessor, isDefaultExportSpan } from "@langfuse/otel";
import { ClaudeAgentSDKInstrumentation } from "@arizeai/openinference-instrumentation-claude-agent-sdk";
import * as ClaudeAgentSDKModule from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk";

const ClaudeAgentSDK = { ...ClaudeAgentSDKModule };
const instrumentation = new ClaudeAgentSDKInstrumentation();
instrumentation.manuallyInstrument(ClaudeAgentSDK);

const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  spanProcessors: [
    new LangfuseSpanProcessor({
      shouldExportSpan: ({ otelSpan }) =>
        isDefaultExportSpan(otelSpan) ||
        otelSpan.instrumentationScope.name ===
          "@arizeai/openinference-instrumentation-claude-agent-sdk",
    }),
  ],
  instrumentations: [instrumentation],
});
sdk.start();

for await (const m of ClaudeAgentSDK.query({ prompt: "...", options: { model: "claude-sonnet-4-6" } })) {
  // ...
}
```

Run any multi-turn agent that uses prompt caching (Claude Sonnet 4.x with system prompt + tools).

## Observed

On the resulting AGENT span (`ClaudeAgent.query`):

| Field | Source | Value |
|---|---|---|
| OTel `attributes.llm.cost.total` | OpenInference (from Anthropic's `result.total_cost_usd`) | **$0.52231845** (correct) |
| OTel `attributes.llm.token_count.total` | OpenInference | 15854 |
| Langfuse `observation.totalCost` | Langfuse | `null` |
| Langfuse `observation.calculatedTotalCost` | Langfuse (= tokens × pricing) | $0.237606 |
| Langfuse `trace.totalCost` (in UI) | Langfuse (rolls up from observations) | $0.237606 (~46% of actual) |

API verification:

```bash
curl -s -u "$LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY:$LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY" \
  "$LANGFUSE_BASE_URL/api/public/observations?traceId=<id>"
```

Returns the AGENT observation with:
- `model: "claude-sonnet-4-6"`
- `usage: { input: 20, output: 13545, total: 13565 }`  ← input tokens clearly missing cache reads
- `calculatedTotalCost: 0.203235`
- `totalCost: null`

The OpenInference instrumentation IS emitting `llm.cost.total` correctly (visible in the Langfuse UI's span "attributes" panel as `attributes.llm.cost.total = 0.52231845`); Langfuse just isn't mapping it.

## Expected

Either:
1. Map `llm.cost.total` → `observation.totalCost` (taking precedence over the tokens-based computation).
2. Surface `llm.cost.total` as a separate displayed field so users can distinguish "model-reported cost" from "Langfuse-computed cost."

Today, accurately measuring spend for any agent run that uses prompt caching requires posting a custom score from the application — that works but adds a layer of indirection and forces every Langfuse integrator using the Claude Agent SDK to re-derive cost client-side.

## Environment

- `@langfuse/otel`: 5.3.0
- `@langfuse/tracing`: 5.3.0
- `@arizeai/openinference-instrumentation-claude-agent-sdk`: 0.2.5
- `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`: 0.3.148
- `@opentelemetry/sdk-node`: 0.218.0
- Langfuse: cloud 
- Node 22 / TS 5.6

title: bug(otel): OpenInference llm.token_count.prompt_details.cache_read/cache_write not recognized by usage extractor
body:
### Describe the bug

Langfuse's OTel ingestion processor does not recognize the **canonical OpenInference attribute names** for prompt-cache tokens. Specifically, the OpenInference semantic conventions define:

* `llm.token_count.prompt_details.cache_read` — tokens read from cache
* `llm.token_count.prompt_details.cache_write` — tokens written to cache

These names are emitted by every official OpenInference instrumentor that supports prompt caching: `openinference-instrumentation-openai`, `openinference-instrumentation-anthropic`, and `openinference-instrumentation-agno`.

In `packages/shared/src/server/otel/OtelIngestionProcessor.ts` (v3.169.0), the `extractGenericGenAiUsageDetails` method has an explicit allow-list of recognized cache-token sub-keys (lines 2530–2539, 2553–2560):

```
cache_read.input_tokens
cache_read_tokens
details.cache_read_tokens
details.cache_read_input_tokens
cache_creation.input_tokens
cache_write_tokens
details.cache_write_tokens
details.cache_creation_input_tokens
```

`prompt_details.cache_read` and `prompt_details.cache_write` are not in this list.

#### Effect

The cache token values **do** reach Langfuse — they end up in `usageDetails` as raw passthrough keys (e.g. `prompt_details.cache_read: 40024`). But because they don't match the resolver's recognized names:

1. They are NOT subtracted from `input` (which can lead to double-counted input on cached calls).
2. They are NOT normalized to `input_cached_tokens` / `input_cache_creation`, the canonical Langfuse internal keys.
3. They are NOT recognized by the cost engine's cache-aware pricing tiers (defined in `worker/src/constants/default-model-prices.json`).
4. They are NOT priced at all — the cost engine prices `input` at full base rate and silently skips the cache keys.

For a workload using `claude-opus-4-6` with prompt caching active, this means Langfuse under-reports cost on cache-heavy observations by \~30% per call, and the `Other usage` section in the UI shows opaque keys instead of a structured "Input cache read / write" breakdown.

#### Evidence — live production data

From a 250-observation sample on a production Langfuse v3.169.0 instance (self-hosted), agent using `agno==2.5.15` + `openinference-instrumentation-agno`:

* 28/250 observations (11.2%) had non-zero cache_read or cache_write
* `usageDetails` keys present: `input`, `output`, `total`, `prompt_details.cache_read`, `prompt_details.cache_write`
* Single-observation example: `input=443`, `output=1806`, `prompt_details.cache_read=40024`, `prompt_details.cache_write=168`
* Langfuse-calculated cost: `$0.047365`
* Anthropic actual cost: `$0.068427` (with cache_read at $0.50/MTok, cache_write_5m at $6.25/MTok)
* Per-call under-report: **30.8%** on heavily cached observations

#### Comparison with the established fix pattern (PR [#12248](<https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/issues/12248>))

PR [#12248](<https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/issues/12248>) fixes the same shape of bug for `pydantic-ai` by adding `gen_ai.usage.details.cache_read_tokens` / `cache_write_tokens` to the resolver. The fix proposed here follows the identical pattern for the OpenInference family of instrumentors.

#### Why this isn't an upstream-OpenInference bug

`llm.token_count.prompt_details.cache_read` is the documented OpenInference semantic-convention name (see `openinference-semantic-conventions/src/openinference/semconv/trace/__init__.py:115`). Changing it upstream would break compatibility with every other observability backend that already speaks the OpenInference convention (Arize Phoenix, Datadog, Honeycomb, etc.). The right place to fix this is in Langfuse's OTel ingestion processor.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Add `agno==2.5.15` and `openinference-instrumentation-agno>=0.1.27,<0.2` to a Python environment, plus an OTel exporter targeting a self-hosted Langfuse (v3.169.0 or any release where the resolver allow-list does not include `prompt_details.cache_*`).
2. Configure agno to enable Anthropic prompt caching (e.g. `cache_system_prompt=True` plus a mixin that attaches `cache_control` to the last tool).
3. Run any agent flow that produces at least 4096 input tokens (Opus minimum for caching) and is invoked twice within 5 minutes (so the second call hits the cache).
4. Inspect the resulting Langfuse observation via the API: `GET /api/public/observations?limit=5&from_start_time=...`
5. Observe `usageDetails` keys: `prompt_details.cache_read` / `prompt_details.cache_write` appear as raw keys; `input_cached_tokens` and `input_cache_creation` are absent; `input` is not reduced by the cached amount; cost is computed only on `input * base_rate + output * output_rate`.

### Langfuse Cloud or self-hosted?

Self-hosted

### If self-hosted, what version are you running?

v3.169.0 (also confirmed by inspecting v3.173.0 source on `main`)

### SDK and integration versions

* `agno==2.5.15`
* `openinference-instrumentation-agno>=0.1.27,<0.2`
* OpenTelemetry SDK as bundled by `openinference-instrumentation-agno`

### Additional information

#### Proposed fix

Two-part change to `packages/shared/src/server/otel/OtelIngestionProcessor.ts::extractGenericGenAiUsageDetails`:

1. Add `prompt_details.cache_read` to the `cacheReadTokens` resolver chain (line 2530).
2. Add `prompt_details.cache_write` to the `cacheCreationTokens` resolver chain (line 2535).
3. Add both keys to the dedup allow-list at lines 2553–2560 so they're not double-emitted.

Plus a unit test asserting that an OpenInference-style span with `llm.token_count.prompt_details.cache_read` / `cache_write` attributes is normalized to `input_cached_tokens` / `input_cache_creation` correctly, with `input` reduced.

I've already implemented and tested this locally against `main` and will open a PR if a maintainer indicates the diagnosis is correct.

#### Related issues / PRs

* langfuse/langfuse#12635 — broader "support cache_read_input_tokens / cache_creation_input_tokens in OTEL generation spans" — this PR addresses the OpenInference subset of that issue.
* [#12248](<https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/issues/12248>) — `fix(otel): correct pydantic-ai v0.7.x+ cache token attribute names` — same structural fix for a different upstream.
* langfuse/langfuse#12994 — inflated token counts with OpenTelemetry Anthropic instrumentor + streaming + images (related but different code path).

### Are you interested in contributing a fix for this bug?

Yes

title: [Bug]: Semantic bleed at section boundaries in VectorStoreIndex on 10‑K filings degrades retrieval precision
body:
### Bug Description

In dense financial filings like 10‑Ks, adjacent sections share a lot of terminology even when they are semantically different (for example, Risk Factors vs Legal Proceedings, or MD&A vs footnotes). When I index full 10‑Ks with VectorStoreIndex and then run targeted QA queries, the retriever often returns chunks from neighboring sections instead of the section that actually answers the question.

This looks like “semantic bleed” around section boundaries: because adjacent sections reuse the same entities, dates, and financial terms, their embeddings are very similar. As a result, top‑k retrieval frequently surfaces neighboring‑but‑irrelevant chunks near section boundaries, which then causes the LLM to answer from the wrong part of the filing and degrades overall QA precision.

### Version

0.11.0

### Steps to Reproduce

Ingest a complete SEC 10‑K filing as a single document and build a VectorStoreIndex over it using standard token-based chunking (for example, 512–1024 tokens with some overlap).

Preserve section headers / item numbers from the filing (for example, “Item 1A. Risk Factors”, “Item 3. Legal Proceedings”, “Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis…”).

Run queries that clearly belong to a specific section, such as:

“How does the company describe its liquidity position in the most recent fiscal year?” (should mainly hit MD&A liquidity discussion)

“What legal proceedings does the company disclose as of the latest filing?” (should mainly hit the Legal Proceedings section)

Inspect the top‑k retrieved nodes and map each node back to its original section header.

You will often see that top‑k includes multiple nodes from immediately adjacent sections that share similar terminology but do not actually answer the query.

### Relevant Logs/Tracbacks

```shell
There is no crash or exception; this is a retrieval‑quality issue. The index and query run successfully, but the retrieved nodes frequently come from neighboring sections that are semantically close in embedding space but incorrect for the user’s question.
```

Enable "Fast (preview)" mode using the toggle in the UI. 5. The observations from step 3 are no longer visible in the list. 6. title: bug: Frontend crashes with client-side exception on browsers where crypto.randomUUID() is unavailable
body:
### Describe the bug

When accessing a self-hosted Langfuse instance from another device on the same LAN, the frontend fails to load on certain browsers with a client-side exception.

The page displays:

`Application error: a client-side exception has occurred while loading <host-ip> (see the browser console for more information).`

The browser console reports an error related to:

`TypeError: crypto.randomUUID is not a function
`
The application becomes unusable after the page loads.

Interestingly, the issue appears browser/environment dependent:

Firefox: reproducible even after enabling the relevant HTTP/security flag.
Chrome: works after enabling the corresponding insecure/private network access flag.
Accessing the same self-hosted instance locally via localhost (through port forwarding on the host machine) works without issues.

This suggests the frontend assumes crypto.randomUUID() is available without a fallback, leading to compatibility issues in certain browser/network configurations.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Deploy Langfuse as a self-hosted instance.
2. Connect another device on the same LAN.
3. Open the Langfuse UI using the server IP and port (e.g. `http://<ip>:<port>`).
4. Log in using valid credentials.
5. Create or upload a trace.
6. Observe the client-side exception

### Langfuse Cloud or self-hosted?

Self-hosted

### If self-hosted, what version are you running?

v3.195.0 OSS

### SDK and integration versions

_No response_

### Additional information

The frontend should either:

- gracefully fall back when` crypto.randomUUID()` is unavailable, or
- detect unsupported environments and provide a meaningful error instead of crashing.

The issue only occurs when accessing the instance remotely over the LAN using the server IP. Accessing the same instance locally via localhost (using port forwarding) works correctly.

### Describe the problem

Following the [Tracing PydanticAI](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/tracing/integrations/listing/pydantic_ai/) tutorial, `mlflow.pydantic_ai.autolog()` raises `ERROR mlflow.pydantic_ai: Error importing pydantic_ai._tool_manager.ToolManager: No module named 'pydantic_ai._tool_manager'`.

This issue does not make tracking integration with pydantic ai unavailable, but the integration with its tool manager is broken. Please refer to **Other info / logs** for root cause analysis.

### Tracking information

(The issue happens before tracking uri is set.)


### Code to reproduce issue

<!-- PLEASE KEEP BACKTICKS AND CHECK PREVIEW -->
```python
import mlflow

# If pydantic-ai >= 1.78.0 is not installed, please install it first
mlflow.pydantic_ai.autolog()
```


### Stack trace

<!-- PLEASE KEEP BACKTICKS AND CHECK PREVIEW -->
The exception does not interrupt the program with Traceback. It is raised by [`mlflow.pydantic_ai.__init__.autolog`](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/9c19354946e81a66ce426ece4b99d2fa00f83141/mlflow/pydantic_ai/__init__.py#L159). The exception case leads to a solution for **back** compatibility, but it is not compatible since `pydantic-ai 1.78.0`.
```
ERROR mlflow.pydantic_ai: Error importing pydantic_ai._tool_manager.ToolManager: No module named 'pydantic_ai._tool_manager'
```


### Other info / logs

<!-- PLEASE KEEP BACKTICKS AND CHECK PREVIEW -->
The [current  mapping](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/blob/9c19354946e81a66ce426ece4b99d2fa00f83141/mlflow/pydantic_ai/__init__.py#L123) logic is to map `pydantic_ai._tool_manager` to: 
- if no exception, it maps to `execute_tool_call`, assuming `pydantic-ai >= 1.63.0`, 
- else, it maps to `handle_call`, assuming `pydantic-ai < 1.63.0`
However, since [`pydantic-ai 1.78.0`](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/releases/tag/v1.78.0), `pydantic_ai._tool_manager` [became public](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/4964/changes/2b64e8da267d6316a7d99649d98a2fbf6fd0ba10), changing to `pydantic_ai.tool_manager`.
As a result, the current mapping key `pydantic_ai._tool_manager.ToolManager` is invalid, it raises the exception and continues. The corresponding function would not work.

This also affects the statement on [mlflow document](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/api_reference/python_api/mlflow.pydantic_ai.html), as the issue exists since 1.78.0.
> Autologging is known to be compatible with the following package versions: 0.1.9 <= pydantic-ai <= 1.79.0. Autologging may not succeed when used with package versions outside of this range.

When using LanceDB with a remote backend in the llama_index integration, the attribute self._metadata_keys remains None if no data is added via the add method. title: bug: Support `cache_read_input_tokens` / `cache_creation_input_tokens` in OTEL generation spans for accurate Anthropic cost calculation
body:
### Describe the bug

**Title:** Support `cache_read_input_tokens` / `cache_creation_input_tokens` in OTEL generation spans for accurate Anthropic cost calculation

## Summary

When OTEL generation spans include `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` in usage details, Langfuse should use Anthropic's cache pricing ($0.30/MTok for cache reads on Sonnet) instead of the full input rate ($3/MTok). Currently all input tokens are priced at the full rate regardless of caching, leading to ~2.5x cost overestimate.

## Evidence

For model `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`:
- Full input rate: $3.00/MTok
- Cache read rate: $0.30/MTok (10x cheaper)
- Cache creation rate: $3.75/MTok

A 46-turn session showed:
- Langfuse calculated cost: **$3.71** (all input at $3/MTok)
- Anthropic's actual cost: **$1.47** (cache-aware billing)
- Overestimate: **2.5x**

## Expected Behavior

When generation spans include cache token breakdowns:
```json
{"cache_read_input_tokens": 41000, "cache_creation_input_tokens": 785, "input": 2500}
```

Langfuse should price:
- `input` tokens at $3.00/MTok
- `cache_read_input_tokens` at $0.30/MTok
- `cache_creation_input_tokens` at $3.75/MTok

## Note

The primary fix is in the LangSmith OTEL exporter (which doesn't currently send cache token data). This issue is for ensuring Langfuse handles the data correctly once it becomes available upstream.
